web_blocks.text: Divisional Architecture & FY25–H1 FY27 Revenue Mix
web_blocks.title: Divisional Architecture & FY25–H1 FY27 Revenue Mix

web_blocks.html: Laurus Labs groups its business into two main divisions: CDMO (Small Molecules and Bio) and Affordable Medicines (Generic APIs and Generic FDFs) [2, 3]. It also breaks out total Anti-Retroviral (ARV) sales across both API and FDF [2, 3]. From FY25 to H1 FY27, the sales mix shifted steadily toward higher-margin CDMO contracts. CDMO rose from 27.6% of sales in FY25 to 30.5% in FY26, then reached 41.9% in H1 FY27 [2, 3].

web_blocks.caption: Segment & Divisional Revenue Mix (FY25, FY26 & H1 FY27)
web_blocks.takeaway: ARV's share of consolidated revenue declined from 46.1% in FY25 to 41.2% in FY26 and 33.2% in H1 FY27 as Small Molecules CDMO scaled +71% YoY in H1 FY27.

web_blocks.text: Segment-by-Segment Walkthrough with Concrete Real-World Examples
web_blocks.title: Segment-by-Segment Walkthrough with Concrete Real-World Examples

web_blocks.html: 1. ARV APIs & Intermediates (₹2,807 Cr combined ARV in FY26; ~33% of H1 FY27): Laurus supplies HIV active ingredients for roughly one-third of the world's treated patients [3, 5]. Example: Take Dolutegravir, Lamivudine, and Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate—the three APIs inside the WHO's first-line HIV pill (TLD) [13]. Global buyers cap finished TLD prices below $45 per patient per year [13]. Laurus makes these APIs at massive scale in Visakhapatnam Units 1, 3, and 4 [6]. It uses flow chemistry and enzymes to cut solvent waste and sells bulk API under annual contracts [6].

2. Generic Finished Dosage Forms — FDF (₹1,987 Cr in FY26, +26% YoY; ₹1,179 Cr in H1 FY27): Laurus turns its own APIs into finished tablets and capsules at Unit 2 in Atchutapuram, which holds over 12 billion units of capacity [6]. Example: Donors like PEPFAR and The Global Fund buy finished TLD (300/300/50 mg) bottles for African clinics [13]. Making both the API and the WHO-approved tablet in-house lets Laurus keep the full margin [6, 13]. Meanwhile, Laurus is expanding into non-ARV US generics, holding 39 USFDA approvals out of 51+ filings [18].

3. Synthesis / CDMO — Small Molecules, Animal Health & Crop Science (₹1,896 Cr in FY26, +38% YoY; ₹1,710 Cr in H1 FY27): Laurus runs 125+ active projects for Big Pharma and biotechs, spanning early clinical drugs to commercial supply [5]. Example: Global animal-health and crop-science firms need dedicated, compliant plants for complex active ingredients [17]. Laurus built LSPL 2 (~350–500 KL) for animal-health steroids and LSPL 4 (~300 KL) for crop-science actives under multi-year contracts [17]. It also launched a >16,000-liter Solid Phase Peptide Synthesis (SPPS) plant in Vizag for peptide drugs [5].

4. Oncology & High-Potency APIs — HPAPIs (within Generic API & CDMO): Targeted cancer drugs and Antibody-Drug Conjugates (ADCs) use toxic payloads that require strict containment [5]. Example: Cancer biotechs and generic firms use Laurus's OEB-4 and OEB-5 suites in Hyderabad and Vizag Unit 5 (161 KL) [5, 6]. Workers handle grams to kilograms inside sealed isolators, earning far higher prices per kilogram than bulk APIs [5, 6].

5. Laurus Bio & ImmunoACT: Laurus Bio (formerly Richcore) generated ₹184 crore in FY26 (+15% YoY) and ₹64 crore in H1 FY27 from its 180 KL Tumkur plant [2, 3, 12]. Example: Vaccine and cell-therapy makers avoid animal serum due to contamination risks [12]. Laurus Bio brews animal-origin-free (AOF) growth factors and enzymes using precision fermentation [12]. Separately, Laurus owns ~34% of IIT Bombay spin-off ImmunoACT, which sells India's NexCar19 CAR-T blood-cancer therapy and runs Phase 2 BCMA trials [5].

book_paragraphs: To see how Laurus Labs actually makes money, picture two completely different factories operating inside the same corporate shell. In the first factory, colossal 3,600-kiloliter reactors in Visakhapatnam churn out metric tons of antiretroviral molecules—Tenofovir, Lamivudine, Dolutegravir—where every penny of solvent recovery matters because global health agencies like PEPFAR and The Global Fund negotiate TLD regimens down below $45 per patient per year.

In the second factory, a scientist in an isolator suit handles grams of a high-potency oncology payload or programs a 16,000-liter Solid Phase Peptide Synthesis train for a global innovator's late-stage clinical drug. Here, the customer is not bidding out a commodity tender every twelve months; they are locking in a multi-year Master Service Agreement because switching a commercial CDMO supplier requires years of re-validation with the USFDA.

Add two adjacent bets that extend that same process-engineering mindset: dedicated blocks for global Animal Health and Crop Science partners (LSPL 2 and LSPL 4), and Laurus Bio's 180-kiloliter precision fermentation tanks in Tumkur brewing animal-origin-free recombinant proteins and growth factors. When you look at H1 FY27—where CDMO jumped 71% year-on-year to 42% of total sales while ARV dropped to 33%—you are watching the second factory steadily overtake the first.

Let us walk inside each of Laurus Labs' five operating engines so you know exactly what leaves the factory gates, who writes the checks, and why the revenue mix looks nothing like it did five years ago.

First, consider the Innovator CDMO / Synthesis division, which just reached ₹1,774 Cr in H1 FY27—41.9% of total company revenue, up from roughly 24% two years ago. Imagine a European animal-health innovator or a global agrochemical major developing a proprietary multi-step molecule with three chiral centers. They cannot hand that route to a low-cost commodity vendor; they need an R&D team of 1,050+ scientists to optimize yield from 12% to 45%, eliminate toxic solvents through continuous-flow chemistry, and then scale from 50-kilogram clinical batches to 50-metric-ton commercial campaigns inside a dedicated, USFDA-audited block. Laurus now manages over 125 active CDMO projects across human health, animal health, and crop science, earning gross margins north of 60%.

Second, look at the legacy Antiretroviral (ARV) API and FDF business, which has deliberately been managed down to 33.2% of H1 FY27 revenue (versus 41.2% in FY26). Here, the customer is not a patent-protected pharma giant; it is the Global Fund, PEPFAR, or national ministries of health procuring life-saving TLD tablets for millions of HIV patients in Sub-Saharan Africa. Pricing is tender-driven and fiercely competitive, which means survival depends on backward integration into Key Starting Materials (KSMs) and massive batch volumes so that every rupee per kilogram saved drops straight to cash flow.

Third, look at Generic Finished Dosage Forms (FDF) outside ARVs—cardiovascular, anti-diabetic, and CNS tablets manufactured in Hyderabad and Vizag for regulated US, European, and Canadian markets. Fourth, consider Oncology and High-Potent APIs (HPAPIs), where specialized containment isolators allow Laurus to synthesize cytotoxic cancer compounds at nanogram occupational-exposure limits—a niche with far fewer qualified global competitors.

Fifth, look at the frontier bets: Laurus Bio in Bengaluru and Tumkur, which uses precision fermentation to manufacture animal-origin-free recombinant proteins and growth factors for biopharma and cultured-food clients, alongside Laurus's strategic stake in ImmunoACT, India's pioneer in indigenous CAR-T cell therapy (NexCAR19). Together, these segments explain both the excitement and the complexity of Laurus Labs: you are underwriting a hybrid of cash-generative generic tenders, high-margin CDMO manufacturing, and long-gestation biotech R&D.

Let us make each of Laurus Labs' business segments tangible so you never confuse an ARV tender tablet with a proprietary CDMO campaign. Picture a global animal-health innovator developing a next-generation parasiticidal molecule. The synthesis requires eight chemical steps, strict stereochemical purity, and zero trace-metal contamination. Laurus's Synthesis division takes that route into its Hyderabad R&D center, redesigns the bottleneck step using enzymatic biocatalysis or continuous-flow chemistry, validates the process at pilot scale, and then dedicates commercial reactor trains in Vizag under a multi-year Master Services Agreement. That single commercial contract can run for a decade at >60% gross margins.

Now contrast that with the legacy ARV business—33.2% of H1 FY27 sales, down from over 60% five years ago. There, Laurus manufactures massive tonnages of Tenofovir, Lamivudine, and Dolutegravir for Global Fund and PEPFAR tenders serving Sub-Saharan Africa. Margins are thin, volumes are predictable, and competitive advantage comes purely from backward integration into Key Starting Materials so that no Chinese intermediate supplier can squeeze you.

Layer on regulated-market Generic FDFs (cardiovascular and diabetic tablets for the US and EU), High-Potent Oncology APIs handled in negative-pressure isolators, and Laurus Bio's precision-fermentation proteins in Tumkur, plus the ImmunoACT CAR-T stake—and you see the full mosaic. Laurus is no longer a one-trick ARV vendor; it is a diversified chemistry and biologics platform whose mix is steadily migrating up the value curve.

Think about the operational contrast inside Laurus Labs' campuses every morning. In one building, massive multi-ton reactors run continuous campaigns of antiretroviral intermediates where every fraction of a percent in solvent recovery decides tender profitability. Across the campus in a dedicated synthesis block, PhD chemists run multi-step asymmetric hydrogenations for a European crop-science or animal-health partner under strict confidentiality.

Meanwhile, in Bengaluru and Tumkur, Laurus Bio's fermentation bioreactors grow recombinant proteins without animal-derived inputs, and partner ImmunoACT treats oncology patients with indigenous CAR-T therapy. Few mid-to-large Indian pharma companies span that breadth of small-molecule, high-potent, and biologics capabilities under one roof.

When you step back and view all five segments together, the strategic logic is unmistakable: ARV and Generic FDF pay the baseline fixed bills and keep large-scale GMP infrastructure humming, while Innovator CDMO, High-Potent Oncology APIs, and Laurus Bio supply the margin expansion and scientific differentiation that global pharma partners actually pay up for.

Put yourself in the shoes of a procurement director at a global animal-health or crop-science company evaluating Laurus Labs today. You are not shopping for the cheapest kilogram of commodity chemical on the planet; you are selecting a long-term manufacturing partner with 1,050+ R&D scientists, proven chiral-chemistry scale-up, and spotless USFDA and EMA inspection history across 11+ sites. That is why the CDMO segment commands >60% gross margins and why its rise to 41.9% of H1 FY27 sales is the single most important structural shift inside the company.

book_callouts.title: Why Mix Shift Matters More Than Headline Topline
paragraphs: A rupee of ARV tender revenue and a rupee of commercial CDMO revenue carry completely different economic DNA. ARV funds fixed overhead and keeps large reactors warm, but CDMO drives gross margins above 60% and creates multi-year customer switching costs.
